posts.title: Why we test before we treat
posts.excerpt: The first hour at Hodoki Clinic is for listening and testing before any treatment starts, so the plan you take home matches the way you actually move.
posts.content:
A first visit at Hodoki Clinic lasts 60 minutes and costs $95. Part of that hour is talk, part of it is movement testing, and part of it is treatment. The order does not change from bay to bay. We listen, we test, and only then do we put hands on you or load a joint. Clara Mendes set that order when she opened the clinic in 2015. It is still how the five treatment bays on the second floor at 41 Alder Street work.

People arrive with a sentence they have already rehearsed. The neck has been tight since a long project. The knee has not felt like their knee since the replacement. The back is fine on the walk from the tram and stiff again by the second meeting. Those sentences matter. They are not yet a plan. Two people can use the same words and move in different ways. One shoulder aches because it has braced beside a mouse for months. Another aches because a surgeon has limited the range on purpose, and the neck is trying to help. Testing is how we tell those apart before we treat either of them.

The tests are plain. We watch you sit, stand, reach, and walk. We measure a joint when the result will change the decision, and we leave the goniometer on the table when it will not. Findings are written down while they are still in front of us. If you have a protocol from your surgeon, the tests stay inside it. Tomasz Wolski will not ask a new knee for a bend the surgeon has deferred. Priya Nair will not ask a repaired shoulder to reach overhead because a desk stretch looks harmless on paper. Staying inside the protocol is a clinical choice. It is not a slower version of the same session.

We test so the first treatment can belong to the same visit. Sixty minutes is enough to do both, and short enough that we cannot hide in paperwork. You should leave having felt a specific change, or having learned that the first idea was wrong. Both are useful. A wrong idea caught in the room costs less than a month of home exercise aimed at the wrong place. The written plan goes out the same day, in ordinary language: what we found, what we did, what to practise, and when to come back. Follow-ups are usually every one to two weeks. At week six we look again and say whether that spacing still fits.

The same order is why we do not sell a package before we have seen you. A block of five follow-ups exists, at $340, for people who already know they want five sessions of 45 minutes within four months. It is optional. A post-surgery rehabilitation session is $90 for 60 minutes. Choosing the first hour does not require you to predict the rest of the year. Elena Duarte can put treatment codes on a receipt for your insurer. She will not guess which insurer will pay it, and she will not ask you to buy the block in order to find out.

Desk problems follow the same rule in a smaller room. Amara Osei can hear that your back hates the chair and still need to see how you hinge. Jonah Reed can hear that the mouse hand aches and still need to see the reach before he treats the forearm. A workstation review, at your office or by video, is a test of the desk rather than of the joint: 45 minutes, $80. We would rather move a screen than hand you a stretch that fights the furniture. Sofia Lindgren's Desk Reset class is practice for people whose plan already exists. It runs 50 minutes for no more than six people, on Tuesday and Thursday at 18:15 and on Saturday at 10:00, at $28. If you have not been assessed, the class is the wrong first door.

None of this tells you how many visits you will need, or how you will feel on a given Friday. Lena, Marcus, and Noor have allowed us to describe their courses elsewhere on this site: six sessions over eight weeks, twelve rehab sessions over fourteen weeks, eight weeks of class plus three follow-ups. Those numbers stay theirs. They are consented composites, told without pain scores. What we repeat, because it is the method and not a result, is the order. Listen. Test. Treat. Write the plan the same day. Review at week six.

If you want that hour, book it online or phone +1 555 0142 300. We are open Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 20:00 and Saturday from 09:00 to 14:00. The last appointment starts one hour before closing. Wear something you can move in. Bring the protocol if a surgeon gave you one. We will not start by telling you to push through. We will start by finding out what is held, and whether it is ready to move.
